newsitem.title: USA: American Indians endorse Clinton for president.
newsitem.headline: American Indians endorse Clinton for president.

text.p: Leaders of tribes representing more than 250,000 American Indians on Tuesday endorsed President Bill Clinton for re-election, saying Clinton had fought for the environment and preserved Indian programmes.

Leonard Garcia, governor of the Navajo Nation's pueblo of Santa Ana in New Mexico, said that when congressional Republicans led by Speaker Newt Gingrich "tried to destroy the budget of the Bureau of Indian Affairs, President Clinton said no."
"When the Gingrich Congress tried to take away our authority to preserve the quality of our air, water and land, President Clinton said no," he said.

Navajo Nation President Albert Hale compared Gingrich's "Contract With America" to Indian treaties broken by the U.S. government and picked up on Clinton's theme that he wants to "build a bridge" to the 21st Century.
"I'm here to tell you that President Clinton has involved and included Indian people in the building of that bridge," Hale said.

The Indian leaders crowded on a stage in a conference room at the Holiday Inn Pyramid where Clinton was preparing for his second and final debate against Republican challenger Bob Dole in San Diego Wednesday night.

Representative Bill Richardson, D-N.M., said another reason Indians back Clinton was because he was instrumental in letting them use feathers from a threatened species, the eagle, for traditional religious practices.
Early in his presidency Clinton played host to a meeting of leaders of American Indians on the White House South Lawn.
Garcia said that in spite of advances, Indians remain the "poorest, least healthy and least educated Americans of all."
"The legacy of our faith in the promises of the United States is poverty, discrimination and ignorance," he said.

Gratified by the endorsement, Clinton said his administration had worked hard to expand tribal sovereignty and self-determination, but he declined to take a position on a bitter dispute between the tribes and New Mexico's state government involving Indian-run casinos.
A number of casinos were closed as a result of a state supreme court ruling and three lawsuits are challenging the decision in federal court.
